title: How this lesson works
text: Before you start · your group ≈ 2 min How this lesson works Slideshow lead Reads each slide aloud and moves the deck forward. Whiteboard scribe Holds the dry erase marker and works problems at the whiteboard. Timekeeper · support Starts each timer and keeps the group on pace. Checker · support Asks "How do we know?" before anyone presses Show answer. Explicit instruction Read it together. Then one person restates it in their own words. title: Ask: steady or changing?
text: See it → describe it Target R5 Ask: steady or changing? A: equal gaps → steady speed. B: growing gaps → increasing speed. Two position patterns A: steady B: speeding up The shape of the position graph helps choose a model. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 06 / 30

title: A picture can show distance

title: Three equations, one model
text: Explicit instruction Target R5 Three equations, one model Equation Useful when… v = v₀ + at You need velocity or time Δx = v₀t + ½at² You know elapsed time v² = v₀² + 2aΔx Time is not given or needed All three assume constant acceleration over the interval. Define the axis before assigning signs. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 09 / 30

title: Constant acceleration toolkit
text: Equations of motion ≈ 15 min Constant acceleration toolkit Velocity v = v₀ + at Position Δx = v₀t + ½at² No time v² = v₀² + 2aΔx Δx means signed displacement. These equations assume constant acceleration. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 10 / 30

title: Which equation?
text: Strategy ≈ 15 min Which equation? 01 List what's given . 02 List what's asked . 03 Find the equation that connects them — and skips what you don't know. 04 Solve, then check units and sign. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 11 / 30

title: Choose from what you know
text: 2026-XJ · No Clock · Graphic novel, page 29 Choose from what you know Nadia explains that the equation must connect what is known to what is needed. The notebook shows v squared equals initial velocity squared plus twice acceleration times displacement. No time is needed. A stop supplies a hidden given: final velocity is zero. Choose an equation from the quantities, not the story. Which known quantities let you find a stopping displacement without first finding time? Part 1 · Defend your equation choice · Write your own answer in Work. Fictional story · Original artwork · Day 8

title: For steady velocity
text: I do · choose the steady model Target R5 For steady velocity Use velocity × time to find displacement. 3 m/s × 2 s = +6 m Follow the cart Equal changes each second. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 13 / 30

title: A repeatable solution structure
text: Explicit instruction Target R5 A repeatable solution structure • Sketch the motion and choose a positive direction. • List known quantities with units and signs. Name the unknown. • Choose an equation containing those quantities. • Rearrange, substitute, and calculate. • Check units, sign, and physical meaning. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 14 / 30

title: For a steady acceleration
text: I do · final velocity Target R5 For a steady acceleration Start at 2 m/s. Gain 1 m/s each second for 3 s. Velocity gain: 1 × 3 = 3 m/s Final velocity: 2 + 3 = 5 m/s Velocity over time Gain first; then add the starting velocity. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 15 / 30

title: Worked braking distance
text: Worked example Target R5 Pairs Worked braking distance A car moves at +20 m/s and brakes at constant −4 m/s² until it stops. How far does it travel? Solve alone · compare as a group · then check. Your turn Work it out on paper. Then press Show answer to check. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 17 / 30

title: Negative acceleration, positive displacement
text: 2026-XJ · No Clock · Graphic novel, page 30 Negative acceleration, positive displacement The novel’s separate practice car brakes from positive thirty meters per second at constant negative six meters per second squared. The calculation gives positive seventy-five meters of braking displacement. Nadia explains that it is still moving forward while slowing; reaction distance is excluded. The novel uses +30 m/s and −6 m/s². The preceding slide uses +20 m/s and −4 m/s². Both end at rest. Why do both displacements stay positive? Check each result using time and average velocity. Part 2 · Check the result another way · Write your own answer in Work. Fictional story · Original artwork · Day 8

title: Check displacement with average velocity
text: I do · displacement Target R5 Pairs An average can make the math easier If acceleration is constant, average the starting and final velocities. (0 + 4) ÷ 2 = 2 m/s Displacement: 2 × 4 = 8 m Same area: triangle or average The shortcut requires constant acceleration. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 19 / 30

title: Different unknowns, different equations
text: 2026-XJ · No Clock · Graphic novel, page 32 Different unknowns, different equations The novel’s train starts from rest with acceleration 0.50 meters per second squared and reaches eighty meters per second in 160 seconds. A separate cart starts at two meters per second and accelerates at 1.5 meters per second squared for four seconds, moving twenty meters. These are separate practice examples. The train’s unknown is time; the cart’s unknown is displacement. Which quantities explain the different equation choices? What constant-acceleration assumption do they share? title: At the top, which quantity is zero?
text: 2026-XJ · No Clock · Graphic novel, page 31 At the top, which quantity is zero? A separate paper model ignores air resistance and chooses upward positive. With launch velocity fifteen meters per second, final vertical velocity zero and acceleration negative 9.8 meters per second squared, the calculation gives a rise of about 11.5 meters. The novel’s paper model launches at 15 m/s; the slide’s example uses 14 m/s. Gravity still acts at the top. Why is the zero assigned to velocity rather than acceleration? Explain the different rises. Part 3 · Transfer the method · Write your own answer in Work. Fictional story · Original artwork · Day 8

title: A method is a choice with a reason
text: Put it in words Target R5 A method is a choice with a reason I chose ___ because the velocity ___. Write units so the result says what you found. A path through the problem 01 Steady velocity Multiply velocity by time. 02 Steady acceleration Find velocity change, or use average velocity. 03 Final position Add displacement to the starting position. Read one step at a time. Day 8 · Constant Acceleration Antocci Physics · 29 / 30
